newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-MPs approve new public procurement laws.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs approve new public procurement laws.

text.p: The European Parliament on Wednesday approved plans to update the European Union's four laws on government procurement contracts, which absorb 11 percent of the EU's gross domestic product or 720 billion Ecus a year of taxpayer's money.

The proposal -- COM(95)107 -- which now goes to the Council of Ministers for formal approval, is designed to bring the existing EU procurement directives (*) into line with a new international Government Procurement Agreement (GPA) agreed during the Uruguay Round of the GATT.
Under the GPA, the EU and its most important trading partners agreed to widen access to contracts offered by publicly owned utilities from January 1 1996 .
One important element of the Commission proposals provoked fierce controversy among Euro-MPs.

The Commission originally proposed a ban on tenderers seeking technical advice from commercial firms when preparing complex contracts, on the grounds that this could give the advisers a competitive advantage in bidding for the contract.
Euro-MPs from across the political spectrum voted to delete the ban on pre-tender consultations from the text, arguing that it would block technical progress.

But the 181-member Christian Democrat EPP group blocked the adoption of provisions that would have forced tenderers to publish -- in the interest of fair competition and transparency -- the names of the firms giving advice.
The transparency clause, proposed by British Socialist Michael Tappin, was supported by 245 votes to 190 but needed an absolute majority of 316 votes to be adopted.

Belgian Christian Democrat Herman Fernand, who advised the EPP on the proposals, told Reuters that blackmail and uncompetitive practices abounded in the battle over the lucrative government contracts, but his party objected to the transparency clause.
"Every day there is blackmail and distortion (of competition)" he said.
"But if there is transparency it makes legal challenges easier," he continued, explaining that powerful utilities regularly tried to sue contracting authorities who selected rival bidders.
"We now have the worst of all possible worlds," Tappin told Reuters after the vote.
The fact that tenderers could now consult firms with a commercial interest in the contract but did not have to publish their names offered "potential for wholesale corruption", he said.
Tappin pledged to revive the issue later this month when the parliament began examining a Commission consultation paper on the future of public procurement.
